concepts.name: Physics and its realm
concepts.statement: Physics is the science concerned with describing the interactions of energy, matter, space, and time, and it is especially interested in what fundamental mechanisms underlie every phenomenon. A surprisingly small and unified set of physical laws explains what we observe.

concepts.name: Model
concepts.statement: A model is a representation of something that is often too difficult or impossible to display directly, such as the planetary model of the atom. It is justified by experiment but accurate only under limited situations, and it lets us picture what we cannot see.

concepts.name: Theory
concepts.statement: To a scientist a theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature, supported by scientific evidence and verified many times by different groups of researchers. It should describe every aspect of any system within its domain, and an experiment that contradicts it means the theory is thrown out or modified.

concepts.name: Law
concepts.statement: A law uses concise language, often a single equation such as F = ma, to describe a generalized pattern in nature that is supported by scientific evidence and repeated experiments. A law describes a single action, whereas a theory explains a whole group of related phenomena.

concepts.name: Scientific method
concepts.statement: The scientific method is the process scientists follow as they inquire about the world: an observation and a question, some research, a hypothesis, an experiment to test it, and a conclusion drawn from the results. The cornerstone is observation, since science must describe the universe as it is.

concepts.name: Classical physics
concepts.statement: Classical physics is the physics that developed from the Renaissance to the end of the 19th century. It is an excellent approximation when matter moves at less than about 1% of the speed of light, when objects are large enough to see with a microscope, and when only weak gravitational fields such as the Earth’s are involved. That is why most of this text deals with it.

concepts.name: Modern physics
concepts.statement: Modern physics consists of two revolutionary theories, relativity and quantum mechanics, which deal with the very fast and the very small. You need relativity above about 1% of the speed of light or in a strong gravitational field, and quantum mechanics for objects smaller than a microscope can show. Their combination, relativistic quantum mechanics, is the best universally applicable theory we have.

concepts.name: Quantum mechanics
concepts.statement: Quantum mechanics is the study of objects smaller than can be seen with a microscope. Together with relativity it makes up modern physics, and it is needed wherever the objects studied are that small.

concepts.name: Physical quantity
concepts.statement: You define a physical quantity either by saying how to measure it or by saying how to calculate it from other measurements. Methods for measuring them define distance and time, whereas average speed is distance traveled divided by time of travel.

concepts.name: Units
concepts.statement: Measurements of physical quantities are expressed in terms of units, which are standardized values. Without them it would be extremely difficult to express and compare measured values in a meaningful way; the two major systems in use are SI units and English units.

concepts.name: Fundamental units
concepts.statement: The most fundamental physical quantities can be defined only in terms of the procedure used to measure them, and their units are called fundamental units. In this text they are length, mass, time, and electric current, measured in the meter, the kilogram, the second, and the ampere.

concepts.name: Derived units
concepts.statement: All other physical quantities, such as force and electric charge, can be expressed as algebraic combinations of length, mass, time, and current; speed, for example, is length divided by time. The units of such quantities are called derived units.

concepts.name: Metric prefixes
concepts.statement: The metric system is convenient for calculation because its units are categorized by factors of 10, and a standard set of prefixes lets the same unit be used over extremely large ranges of values. Distances in meters suit construction, kilometers suit air travel, and nanometers suit optical design, with no need to invent new units.

concepts.name: Order of magnitude
concepts.statement: The order of magnitude of a value is the power of 10 that sets its scale. The numbers 800 and 450 can both be written as a number times 10², so they are of the same order of magnitude; the diameter of an atom is of order 10⁻¹⁰ m and the diameter of the Sun of order 10⁹ m.

concepts.name: Conversion factor
concepts.statement: A conversion factor is a ratio expressing how many of one unit are equal to another unit, such as 1000 meters in 1 kilometer or 60 seconds in 1 minute. Multiplying by the factor that cancels the unwanted unit leaves the desired unit in its place.

concepts.name: Converting units
concepts.statement: To convert, list the units you have and the units you want, find the conversion factor between them, and multiply so that the units cancel. If the factor is written upside down the units do not cancel, so checking the units of the answer is part of the method.

concepts.name: SI units
concepts.statement: SI units, also known as the metric system, are the international system of units that scientists in most countries have agreed to use, named for the French Système International. This text uses them almost exclusively.

concepts.name: English units
concepts.statement: English units, also known as the customary or imperial system, are the units historically used in nations once ruled by the British Empire and still widely used in the United States, such as feet, gallons, and pounds.

concepts.name: Second
concepts.statement: The second is the SI unit of time. It is defined as the time required for 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the cesium atom.

concepts.name: Meter
concepts.statement: The meter is the SI unit of length. It is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

concepts.name: Kilogram
concepts.statement: The kilogram is the SI unit of mass. It was once defined as the mass of a platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris, and since 2019 it is defined in terms of the second, the meter, and Planck's constant.

concepts.name: Length
concepts.statement: Length is one of the fundamental physical quantities, the distance between two points. Its SI unit is the meter.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.statement: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the correct value for that measurement. Three measurements of 11.1, 11.2 and 10.9 inches of paper that is 11.0 inches long are accurate; a measurement of 12 inches is not.

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.statement: The precision of a measurement system refers to how close the agreement is between repeated measurements made under the same conditions, that is, to the spread of the measured values. A measuring system can be accurate but not precise, or precise but not accurate.

concepts.name: Uncertainty
concepts.statement: Uncertainty is a quantitative measure of how much your measured values deviate from a standard or expected value, a disclaimer on the number: 45,000 miles plus or minus 500. All measurements contain some uncertainty, from the measuring device, the skill of the person, irregularities in the object, and anything else that affects the outcome.

concepts.name: Percent uncertainty
concepts.statement: One way to express uncertainty is as a percent of the measured value: the uncertainty divided by the value, times 100%. A bag of apples weighed at 5.1 lb with an uncertainty of 0.4 lb has a percent uncertainty of 8%.

concepts.name: Method of adding percents
concepts.statement: There is an uncertainty in anything calculated from measured quantities. When the measurements going in have small uncertainties, the percent uncertainty in a quantity calculated by multiplication or division is the sum of the percent uncertainties in the items used to make the calculation: a floor 4.00 m by 3.00 m, known to 2% and 1%, has an area of 12.0 m² known to 3%.

concepts.name: Significant figures
concepts.statement: When we express measured values we can list only as many digits as the measuring tool gave us, and the last digit written down is the first digit with some uncertainty. Counting the digits from the first measured digit on the left through the last on the right gives the number of significant figures, and zeros are significant except when they serve only as placekeepers.

concepts.name: Significant figures in multiplication and division
concepts.statement: For multiplication and division, the result should have the same number of significant figures as the quantity having the least significant figures entering into the calculation. A circle whose radius is known to two figures has an area known to two figures, even though π is good to at least eight.

concepts.name: Significant figures in addition and subtraction
concepts.statement: For addition and subtraction, the answer can contain no more decimal places than the least precise measurement. Potatoes weighed on scales good to 0.01 kg, 0.001 kg and 0.1 kg add up to a mass that can be given only to the tenth of a kilogram.

concepts.name: Area
concepts.statement: Area is the size of a surface, found for a rectangle as its length times its width. Its SI unit is the square meter.

concepts.name: Making an approximation
concepts.statement: Physicists, other scientists and engineers often need approximations or “guesstimates” for a quantity, based on formulae whose inputs are known only to limited accuracy. Scaling up from a known quantity, such as the height of a person, gives an estimate good to an order of magnitude, which is enough to rule out unrealistic numbers and to guide an approach.

concepts.name: Volume
concepts.statement: Volume is the space an object occupies, found for a box as its length times its width times its height. Its SI unit is the cubic meter.

concepts.name: Approximation
concepts.statement: An approximation is an estimated value based on prior experience and reasoning.
